I am a 52-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I have been farming this land for over thirty years. I have five mu of flat, good-quality land on the North China Plain. Here, if you do not plant winter wheat followed by summer maize, you are leaving money on the table — this double-cropping system is what our soil and climate were made for. The wheat is already in the ground from last October, and now that spring has arrived, my main job is to manage the green-up, top-dress with urea at the reviving stage, and irrigate three or four times before the June harvest. I always use improved wheat varieties like the local Jimai types because they are reliable and handle our winters well. For the summer maize, I will plant hybrid Zhengdan 958 or something similar right after the wheat comes out — it matures fast and yields well. I will rotary till before maize sowing to clean up the wheat stubble and level the field, even though some neighbors are trying no-tillage; I trust rotary tillage because it controls weeds and gives the maize a clean start. I will apply compound fertilizer as a base and top-dress nitrogen at the big trumpet stage. The maize usually gets two irrigations — one if the sowing is dry and another at filling — because the summer rains in July and August usually do most of the work. I keep my pesticide use practical: herbicide in spring for the wheat, plus fungicide and insecticide if I see aphids or rust, and for the maize, a pre-emergence herbicide and one or two sprays for corn borers. This is my plan.
